fact.claim: Morningstar looked at the S&P 500 from January 1990 to March 13, 2026. An investor who missed its 10 best days earned about 2.40% less per year than one who stayed invested the whole time. The best days sat close to the worst ones: the median gap between a 10-worst day and a 10-best day was seven days. There is one exception. Skipping the 10 worst days would have added 2.66% a year, but since the two kinds of day come so close together, getting out after a bad day usually means missing the rebound too.

caption:
Missing the market's 10 best days cost about 2.4% a year.

Morningstar looked at the S&P 500 from January 1990 to March 13, 2026. Someone who missed its 10 best days earned about 2.40% less per year than someone who just stayed in.

The catch is where those days sit. The median gap between one of the 10 worst days and one of the 10 best was seven days. So if you get out after a bad day, you'll usually miss the bounce too.

Yes, skipping the 10 worst would've added 2.66% a year. But you can't tell which day is which until it's over, and that's the trap. This is US stocks, not the TSX, and past results aren't a promise.
